title: What is known about 1RB0LB_1RC0LD_0LA1RD_1LC1LE_1LF0RE_1LD---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LB_1RC0LD_0LA1RD_1LC1LE_1LF0RE_1LD---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves two of the machine's fast moves and its halting situation (kernel) and no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide); the C simulator finds no halt in 109 steps.

What it does. The tape has two regular parts. On the left a 26-cell word is repeated (w = 1111 000 1 000 1 000 111111 0 1 000), and the number of copies grows by one every few hundred thousand steps late in the run. On the right a finer pattern of short blocks grows too. Between them is an irregular boundary region where the head does its work in zig-zags of 50 to 100 cells; it never sweeps the whole tape in one go.
Where a halt would come from. Only F reading a 1 halts, and F is entered from E reading a 0; so 1 0 D>1 halts (halt_D). In the first 2·106 steps D reads a 1 233,188 times, never with 1 0 to its left.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 10,084 cells have been visited and 4,463 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.384). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.378).

claims.title: Every way to a halt
claims.text: Two steps before any halt the machine is in 1 0 D>1; no other configuration halts within three steps.

claims.title: Two fast moves
claims.text: E moving right erases a run of 1s (erase); D moving left turns each 100 into 111 (fill), for any length.

claims.title: The halting situation
claims.text: 1 0 D>1 halts after two steps; F is entered only from E reading a 0.

claims.title: Never close to halting
claims.text: In the first 106 steps F reads a 0 86,468 times, and in the first 2·106 steps D never reads a 1 with 1 0 to its left.

claims.title: Two periodic regions
claims.text: Late in the run (10<sup>6</sup> to 2·10<sup>6</sup> steps) the left part of the tape is the 26-cell word w repeated 12 to 20 times (at the moments the head reaches a new cell on the left), then an irregular region, then a right part made of short blocks.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The next step is the rule by which the boundary region turns right-hand material into copies of w.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. Two regular patterns grow on either side of a boundary where the head works. This page runs the machine in your browser.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 10,084 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Two crystals and a boundary
html: The space-time diagram looks like two crystals growing from a seam. On the left a 26-cell word repeats,

and at the moments the head reaches a new cell on the left the tape starts 0 1 000 wn, with n = 14 after 1.2·106 steps and 20 after 1.9·106. On the right the tape is a finer pattern of blocks 1000, 11, 11111 separated by 00. Between the two is an irregular region a few dozen cells wide.

The head never sweeps the whole tape. It works in zig-zags of 50 to 100 cells around the boundary, and every so often runs out to an end to add a cell there. Its fast moves are simple: E erases a run of 1s moving right (erase), and D moving left fills each 100 into 111 (fill).

The machine halts only from 1 0 D>1 (halt_D): D keeps the 1 and steps left in state E, E writes a 1 and steps left in state F, and F on a 1 has no transition. The pattern 1 0 to the left of D never occurs in the run. Showing why, through the exact rule of the boundary, is the open step.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.384). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.378).
After 109 steps the tape spans 10,084 cells (6,672 left of the start, 1,077 right), with a density of 1s of 0.443.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: two periodic regions with a working boundary (zig-zag), period 26 on the left
summary: Two periodic regions, a 26-cell word repeated on the left and a finer pattern on the right, meet at an irregular boundary where the head works in short zig-zags; both grow like the square root of time. Open.
